data.title: Hradec near Prievidza – a Celtic and Slavic hillfort on a rocky hill
data.excerpt: The hillfort above the village of Hradec was discovered by Š. Janšák and excavated in 1956. Its small summit plateau, bounded by two andesite rocks and closed off by a low rampart, yielded finds of the La Tène period as well as of the 8th–9th century, among them a gilded bronze belt mount with a bird motif probably made in the Salzburg workshops around 800.

children.text: The Slavic hillfort in the immediate vicinity of the village of Hradec (Prievidza district), to the south of the village, was discovered by Š. Janšák, who was also the first to publish a brief description of it. In 1956 an archaeological excavation was carried out at the hillfort.

blocks.caption: A plan of the hillfort by Š. Janšák from 1928
blocks.alt: A plan of the hillfort by Š. Janšák from 1928

children.text: The hillfort stands on a fairly steep rocky hill whose eastern part has been partly damaged by an old quarry. The top of the hill forms a small plateau, bounded on the north and north-west by two steep andesite rocks. On the remaining sides the plateau is closed off by a low rampart which joins the two rocks in an elongated arc. Roughly in the middle the rampart is interrupted by a gateway, with both arms of the rampart drawn inwards into the enclosure. During the excavations no structural features could be uncovered by trenches on the summit of the hillfort. The rampart consisted of large andesite and tuff stones mixed with black soil and at the time of the excavation reached a height of about 50 cm. The rampart was heaped up by digging a narrow hollow on its inner side. The occupation layer yielded objects of the La Tène period (the Late Iron Age – on the territory of present-day Slovakia associated above all with the Celts and the Dacians) and then of the 8th–9th century, that is, of the period of the Principality of Nitra and Great Moravia.

The La Tène period is represented above all by finds of pottery sherds from barrel-shaped, vase-shaped and storage vessels. In the Late Iron Age, specifically around the middle of the 1st century BC, a Celtic–Dacian hillfort therefore extended over the site, or more precisely a Celtic one with certain Dacian elements. It is the northernmost hillfort in which Dacian influences can be detected.

Hradec belongs among the numerous hillforts in the mountainous part of Slovakia, set on steep conical hills or inaccessible crags and characterised by their small area. The insufficient investigation of these hilltop settlements still does not allow their original function to be determined with certainty. They may, however, have been the seats of a group of people with an exceptional social and economic standing. In the case of Hradec, though, finds of dwelling and farm features are lacking. The trial excavation at Hradec produced no finds that would confirm that the hillfort was more permanently occupied in the time of the Celts. Hradec must therefore also be regarded as a refuge and guard hillfort for a nearby settlement. The building of these small, and not infrequently probably temporary, fortifications certainly testifies to a troubled age and to movements of population. Small fortlets, which were often built in the immediate vicinity of extensive Late Hallstatt hillforts (Mních near Ružomberok, Skalka above Vyšný Kubín), confirm that individual settlements in this territory at the end of the La Tène period and during the Roman period were much smaller in area than the settlements of the preceding period.

The advantageous position of the hillfort was used in the Early Middle Ages by the Slavs as well, as is shown by finds of typical Slavic pottery and of other objects, on the basis of which the Great Moravian period can be dated. Among the metal objects there were a deltoid arrowhead with a tang and a small belt mount, as well as part of the handle of a bucket and an object of small-chisel shape with a socket. Slavic sherds decorated with a wavy line were also found, together with a well-preserved knife, part of a scythe from the turn of the 8th and 9th centuries and several further objects.

The most remarkable find from the hillfort is undoubtedly a small gilded bronze belt mount. The mount consists of two escutcheon-shaped fields set horizontally opposite each other and joined by a bar in which there are holes for three rivets. The mount has an elongated rectangular shape (dimensions 18 × 40 mm). It bears a stylised motif of a bird with its head turned back. The mount is a fine piece of metal casting (thickness 1–1.5 mm) whose effect is emphasised by deep chip-carving and gilding, aimed at heightening the optical effect of light and shade. Comparable mounts are classed within the circle of early Carolingian products with animal ornament following Anglo-Saxon models and dated to the beginning of the 9th century. A similar mount was found, for example, at Modrá, but also in Perugia. Archaeologists date its making to around 800, and it was probably made somewhere in the Salzburg workshops. It may have reached the territory of Slovakia through trade, but also as war booty, or as a gift to a local Slavic nobleman.

The excavation at Hradec did not prove that the Slavs built its fortification; it is more likely that they repaired and reused the older Celtic ramparts. It is clear, however, that in the time of Great Moravia the hillfort served as a guard point lying beside an important route that led through the Nitra region into Turiec and from there as far as the Kraków area. In the surroundings of Prievidza, as well as of Turiec, there may have been important tribal centres at the beginning of the 8th century, which were gradually incorporated into the Principality of Nitra.
